articles.title: He watched children his age give up their dreams to work: 15 years later, this Andhra Pradesh man is bringing hope to 90,000 children across 110 villages, fighting to ensure no child has to sacrifice their childhood for survival
articles.summary: Born to daily-wage agricultural labourers, Bethala Veera Swami grew up seeing how poverty could stand between children and education.
articles.body: Born to daily-wage agricultural labourers, Bethala Veera Swami grew up seeing how poverty could stand between children and education. Today, the mechanical engineer, who continues to work in Abu Dhabi, is helping rural children access learning opportunities through PARD India, the nonprofit he founded with childhood friends. Growing up in the rural village of Yernagudem, Bethala Veera Swami saw how a family's financial circumstances could determine a child's future. Children with dreams of continuing their education sometimes had to leave school and work to support their families; some children entered the workforce. Others left school because there was little support at home or because they had fewer opportunities to learn beyond the classroom. For a child growing up in a household dependent on daily-wage agricultural labour, the consequences of poverty were not an abstract problem. They were visible in the lives of people around him.Years later, those experiences would help shape an initiative aimed at ensuring that fewer children face the same choices. Swami founded Pragathi Association for Rural Development (PARD India) in 2011 with childhood friends from Yernagudem village in Andhra Pradesh. According to the organisation's profile on Daan.org, PARD India reports that its programmes have influenced 90,494 children and reached more than 550 communities, with a presence in 110 villages. These figures are self-reported by the organisation and should not be interpreted as an independently audited count of children directly supported.Swami's journey took him from rural Andhra Pradesh into engineering, eventually leading to work in Abu Dhabi. But his professional career did not mean leaving his home community's challenges behind. Instead, he continued to lead an organisation designed to make education and other opportunities more accessible to children growing up in circumstances similar to those he had witnessed.Starting with 50 childrenPARD India was registered on January 13, 2011, and began its first After School Education Programme in August that year. The programme started with 50 children in Classes 4 and 5 at the government school Swami had attended as a child, according to the organisation's published programme information.The idea was simple: children should have access to additional academic support even when their circumstances at home make studying difficult. The programme provides guided learning after regular school hours, covering subjects such as mathematics, English and science, alongside moral education, computer skills and extracurricular activities.The classes operate six days a week, according to the programme account. Teachers also monitor attendance and coordinate with parents and volunteers when children miss classes, helping identify problems that might eventually lead to a dropout.For children who do not have access to private tuition or additional learning resources, this kind of support can make a difference. It also offers a way for communities to identify students who may be struggling before they leave school altogether.An engineer's personal investment in rural educationOne of the most striking parts of Swami's work is that he continued pursuing his engineering career while helping build PARD India. His professional life in Abu Dhabi and his commitment to rural education have developed alongside each other. In 2012, he personally contributed ₹8 lakh to establish a Village Knowledge Centre in Yernagudem, equipping it with 15 computers. The centre was intended to bring digital learning opportunities to a rural community where access to technology could otherwise be limited.PARD India's Village Knowledge Centre Programme document says the initiative was launched on August 26, 2012, to bridge the digital divide between rural and urban communities. It provided free computer and internet training to children, students, young people and working professionals, along with career guidance, personality development and support with online job searches.The centre operated for nearly eight years before its equipment became outdated, according to the account of the initiative. The programme's ambition, however, went beyond teaching children how to use computers. Digital skills could also help them access educational resources, explore career options and prepare for employment. For Swami, the investment represented an effort to bring opportunities closer to the village rather than expecting young people to overcome every barrier on their own.Helping children stay in educationPARD India subsequently expanded its work through scholarship and academic support programmes. The V-Kid Scholarship Programme and the V-Kid Knowledge Boost Programme were introduced in 2014, according to the organisation's programme account. The scholarship initiative is intended to help disadvantaged students continue their education, from primary school through graduation. Its focus includes children who have lost one or both parents and those from economically vulnerable families.The need for such assistance extends beyond school fees. Books, transport, food and other education-related expenses can become difficult for families dependent on irregular or low incomes. When these costs compete with household essentials, children may be pressured to stop studying.Financial assistance, combined with academic guidance, can help reduce some of that pressure. PARD India's approach brings these interventions together with after-school education and digital learning, seeking to address several of the barriers that can prevent children from reaching their potential.The organisation's 2023-24 annual report records 206 children benefiting from its After School Education Programme during that financial year and 58 students receiving direct support through its Quality and Value Education Programme. These are figures for particular programmes during one reporting period, not the total number of children reached since the organisation began.Extending support beyond the classroomPARD India's work has also expanded into nutrition, community support and livelihood development. The organisation's programmes include food assistance for people in need, sewing training for women and environmental initiatives. Its 2023-24 annual report records 2,540 cooked meals provided through its Hearts of Serving the Humanity Programme during the year. It also reports that 112 women received training through its Power of Sewing initiative, which aims to develop skills that can support economic self-reliance.These programmes address different needs, but they are connected by the circumstances in which children grow up. A student may struggle to concentrate on schoolwork when a household is facing food insecurity or financial uncertainty. Supporting families and strengthening livelihood opportunities can therefore complement efforts to keep children in education.The organisation's published profile reports that its initiatives have influenced 90,494 children across more than 110 villages in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The initiative now wants to reach 20,000 children across 150 villages by 2030 and provide more than eight million hours of free education. It also plans to introduce STEM-based projects in government schools, expand scholarships from Class 1 through graduation, and develop Village Knowledge Centres with computer- and AI-enabled literacy and skills training.You use AI every day. articles.summary: In 2015, a German couple travelled to India without a return ticket to Europe.
articles.body: In 2015, a German couple travelled to India without a return ticket to Europe. They came in search of a deeper spiritual connection and today they are settled here with two kids. They moved to Mayapur, a small pilgrimage town in West Bengal, and today call it their home. The couple is raising two kids, exploring the region's spiritual and cultural traditions and also running a small business. They document their everyday experiences through their social media platform, ‘I Love Mayapur’.Meet the Germans living in IndiaThe family, which originally comes from Germany, has been living in Mayapur since 2015, according to their Instagram account. What makes their story particularly unique for travellers is that their journey offers a glimpse into an unexplored side of India that is often experienced by outsiders. The spiritual communities, everyday rituals and local festivals.How a spiritual journey brought them to West BengalAs per their account, the couple's connection with India began with an interest in the Hare Krishna movement and the teachings of ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness).On their official About Us page, it says,“When we first came to Mayapur, we immediately felt at home. The peaceful atmosphere, the warm-hearted community, and the presence of our beloved Sri Sri Radha Madhava Mandir inspired us deeply. Over the years, Mayapur has become more than just our home — it’s our heart”.Their quest for spirituality led them to Mayapur."We wanted to move in a little bigger community," one of them explained in their Instagram video. Mayapur stole their hearts and the family had found a place where spirituality was not restricted to occasional temple visits but it was right there, when they would open the door.Their everyday life in MayapurFor the family, living in Mayapur means following a routine that revolves around Krishna, spirituality, and dance and community participation.In the videos shared on their social media, they describe that their day generally begins early with chanting and devotional practices. The family cleans and prepares for the day together before the children leave for school. Now, they have friends in Mayapur.Ended last link with GermanyIn one of the Instagram videos, the man said he ended the last link with Germany recently where he had a catering business.Now the family lives in Mayapur and documents their life on social media. The family also shares videos on YouTube.Their work has gradually expanded beyond documenting their lives. According to their website, they started an online shop in 2022, selling products inspired by Mayapur, Indian traditions and devotional practices.Mayapur: The spiritual town that became their homeMayapur is a beautiful spiritual town located in West Bengal's Nadia district, near Nabadwip. The town is one of the most important pilgrimage destinations for followers of Gaudiya Vaishnavism and is regarded as the birthplace of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, the 16th-century saint associated with the spread of Krishna bhakti.The town is also home to the international headquarters of ISKCON and attracts devotees from different parts of India and abroad. The West Bengal Tourism Department states that more than a million pilgrims visit the destination annually.Places to visit in MayapurSri Mayapur Chandrodaya MandirISKCON templeSrila Prabhupada's SamadhiWhen here, visitors can also enjoy a boat ride along the Ganga and experience the river landscape.How to reach MayapurThe nearest airport is Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport in Kolkata.Mayapur is nearly 129 km from Kolkata by road, with the journey taking around four hours, depending on traffic.The town does not have its own railway station. Those travelling by train can take a train towards Nabadwip Dham and continue by road to Mayapur.A life beyond the usual tourismFor some, Mayapur is a destination for a few days of temple visits, boat rides and spiritual exploration. For this German family, it became a place to build relationships, raise children, pursue a livelihood and establish roots.Their official website also reveals that they are working on a new home project near the Jalangi River. The family additionally offers guided tours through Sudevi, who shares lesser-known places, local stories and cultural experiences with visitors.Perhaps that is what makes their journey particularly interesting: they did not simply discover a destination in India; they decided to make a life around everything that made them fall in love with it.You use AI every day. articles.title: This mayor crusaded against cartels in Mexico. Now his assassination haunts his city
articles.summary: URUAPAN, Mexico (AP) — Three armored cars and two military trucks packed with armed bodyguards carry Mayor Grecia Quiroz through the streets of Uruapan, the...
articles.body:
URUAPAN, Mexico (AP) — Three armored cars and two military trucks packed with armed bodyguards carry Mayor Grecia Quiroz through the streets of Uruapan, the Mexican city where her partner was gunned down during Day of the Dead celebrations nearly a year ago.

Carlos Alberto Manzo gained a reputation as a mayor crusading against cartels, a thorn in the side of criminals and political powerbrokers. But a year later — even as Quiroz has succeeded him and vowed to continue his fight — the targeted assassination casts a pall over a region long haunted by violence.

"No one can fill his void," said Quiroz, who is escorted around the clock by 60 federally appointed bodyguards. "I'm extremely worried that if tomorrow, something happens to me, what will (my children) do without a father and a mother?"

Manzo was among at least 13 mayors killed across Mexico in the two years since Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took office, according to an Associated Press tally based on official reports. That compares with 23 sitting mayors killed during the previous administration's six years in office, according to civil society groups.

The killings present a challenge for Sheinbaum as the Trump administration presses her government to crack down on cartels and root out corruption in local governments.

'Fighting to clean up this filth that's killing us all'

Political violence has long been part of Mexico's cartel conflict , but it rarely touches the highest ranks of government. Cartels instead target local leaders, either corrupting them or killing those who stand in their way. Such killings often silence voices that threaten or interfere with cartel profits, said Miguel Meza, a researcher at the investigative organization Narcopoliticos.

In Uruapan, 250 miles (400 km) west of Mexico City, Manzo's killing has sowed fear and uncertainty within his grassroots opposition Sombrero Movement, where he's gone from leader to martyr. The aftermath has fueled a bitter political fight dividing Mexico's central Michoacan state over who was behind his death. At the same time, the city has been marked with a recent burst of violence as some criticize Quiroz for failing to carry on her partner's fight against crime.

"They didn't just kill the mayor, they killed the person who was leading this fight against cartels, a symbolic leader," Meza said.

Those close to Manzo long feared that his campaign against criminal groups would inevitably end exactly as it did: with a bullet in his chest.

In Michoacan, where cartels often wield more influence than the government, Manzo gained political notoriety for taking the fight against cartels into his own hands and also openly challenged Mexico's ruling party, Morena, up until the week of his death.

He was often criticized for heavy-handed tactics that became as central to his image as mayor as the white sombrero always perched on his head. That included publicly instructing police to use lethal force on criminals resisting arrest or attacking civilians. He personally directed patrols, searches and arrests, urged parents to report their children's criminal activity and publicized confrontations with criminals on his social media.

"We're fighting to clean up this filth that's killing us all," Manzo said in one video.

A public murder triggers a political rift

The public assassination of Manzo in the city's crowded main plaza, cloaked in marigold flowers, shocked the country on a day when many criminal groups quietly set down their weapons as families honor their dead.

It also triggered a political feud marked by rival factions slinging accusations at one another of exploiting Manzo's death to profit politically ahead of local elections.

Federal and state authorities have blamed the killing on one of Mexico's most powerful cartels, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel , or CJNG, one of the more than 20 criminal groups designated foreign terrorist organizations by the Trump administration. Quiroz accused state officials in Sheinbaum's party who were long at odds with Manzo and Quiroz's political movement and criminal groups of being behind the death.

As Quiroz prepared the city for Day of the Dead this week, she said she was haunted by the memory of Manzo meticulously preparing the previous year's celebration.

"It's all come back to me like a countdown of what happened that last week he was alive," she said. "He poured his body and soul into this."

Authorities have detained 34 people in connection with Manzo's killing as state prosecutors have described a complex conspiracy that they say extended to Manzo's inner circle.

Among those detained are seven of the mayor's bodyguards who were with him when he was attacked, members of his government accused of leaking his movements, and Manzo's own godson, who is accused of helping plan his assassination, according to prosecutors.

On Thursday, prosecutors announced the detention of the city's current secretary of welfare on accusations of obstruction of justice. They said she was related to two alleged CJNG members arrested for Manzo's killing.

Quiroz herself has also come under scrutiny as she has declined to turn over Manzo's cellphone to prosecutors. Manzo's brother, a member of Morena in the state government now at odds with Quiroz, has accused her of defending some of those detained after the killing.

"I can't directly accuse her," Juan Manzo said. "But the reality is that she has covered for many of those responsible for the murder of her children's father. She has not been transparent during the investigation."

Quiroz has denied the accusations, and said her family was "betrayed" by those closest to them.

"Slandering us, resorting to dirty tactics and low blows has never stopped us and never will," she told members of her political movement.

'We cannot allow violence to become our new normal'

As the political rift has deepened, Uruapan has experienced a surge of violence in recent weeks.

Just over the weekend, a masked man on a motorcycle shot two women working at a taco stand, killing one. The same day, local media reported that police found two men, one who had died, in an avocado field with severe burns and signs of torture. State authorities said they have documented 17 killings, eight gunshot injuries, four attacks on businesses and homes and a series of robberies in October.

The violence prompted Quiroz to request help from Sheinbaum's government.

"We cannot allow violence to become our new normal," she wrote Sunday on X. "Uruapan deserves to live in peace."

On Tuesday, state authorities sent 200 law enforcement officers to boost security in the city.

Some residents, including store owner David Vázquez, said extortions by local mafias have mounted since Manzo was killed, forcing his family to temporarily close down their business.

He expressed resentment watching the fleet of state bodyguards escorting Quiroz, saying "they only protect her and her family." Others said that they had not been affected by the violence and believed Quiroz was doing her best in the face of trauma.

Meanwhile, Manzo's presence still looms over Uruapan. Posters and busts paying tribute to him paint the plaza where he was killed. His grave, open to the public, is covered with flowers, food offerings and white sombreros.

"Not a single step backward," the headstone reads.

Janetsky reported from Mexico City. Associated Press photojournalist Eduardo Verdugo Tucto contributed to this report from Uruapan, Mexico.

articles.title: A man paid just $60 for two paintings at an Arizona estate sale in 1996, then discovered they were genuine Martin Johnson Heade artworks worth $1.072 million; the sellers later went to court but lost
articles.summary: In 1996, Carl Rice attended an Arizona estate sale, spotted two framed oil paintings priced at $30 each, and paid the $60 asking price without expecting
articles.body: In 1996, Carl Rice attended an Arizona estate sale, spotted two framed oil paintings priced at $30 each, and paid the $60 asking price without expecting anything extraordinary. He liked the subject matter of one painting and the frame of the other, but assumed that paintings sold so cheaply by a professionally managed estate could not be original works by a major artist. That assumption proved spectacularly wrong. The paintings were later authenticated as works by Martin Johnson Heade, a celebrated 19th century American painter, and sold at Christie’s for a combined $1.072 million. The story did not end with the auction. Martha Nelson’s estate, whose personal representatives had organised the sale, later sued Rice and his wife Anne in an effort to undo the transaction. The estate argued that both sides had made a mutual mistake about the paintings’ value and that enforcing the sale would be unconscionable. But the Arizona Court of Appeals disagreed, affirming the lower court’s decision and leaving the Rices with the proceeds. The case remains a striking example of how estate sales can hide extraordinary value, and of how the law treats a bargain made in good faith.A $60 purchase at an estate saleAccording to Justia U.S. Law, After Martha Nelson died in February 1996, her estate’s personal representatives, Kenneth Newman and Edward Franz, hired Judith McKenzie-Larson to appraise the personal property before an estate sale. McKenzie-Larson told them that she did not appraise fine art and that they would need another appraiser if any fine art were found. She did not report finding any, and relying on her appraisal, the representatives priced and sold the estate’s belongings.Carl Rice responded to a newspaper advertisement and attended the public sale. He paid the estate’s asking price of $60 for two oil paintings. Although he had bought and sold some art before, he was not a trained or sophisticated collector. Court records note that he had never made more than $55 on a single piece and had previously purchased works that turned out to be frauds, forgeries, or pieces by lesser known artists.Rice later said he assumed the paintings were not originals because of the low price and because the estate appeared to be professionally managed. Still, something about them caught his attention. He was drawn to the subject of one painting and the frame of the other, and after bringing them home he compared the signatures with examples in a book of artists’ signatures. The signatures appeared similar to that of Martin Johnson Heade.The discovery that changed everythingFollowing their usual practice, the Rices sent photographs of the paintings to Christie’s in New York to see whether they might be Heade’s work. Christie’s authenticated both paintings, Magnolia Blossoms on Blue Velvet and Cherokee Roses, as genuine works by Heade. The auction house then offered to sell them on consignment. Christie’s later sold the paintings at auction for $1,072,000. After deducting the buyer’s premium and commission, the Rices received $911,780. They paid $337,000 in income taxes on the profit in 1997, bought a home, created a family trust, and used part of the money for living expenses. What had begun as an ordinary $60 estate sale purchase had become a life changing windfall, as per Justia U.S. Law.Magnolia Blossoms on Blue Velvet is an oil on canvas measuring 15 by 24 inches and signed “M.J. Heade” in the lower right. Christie’s records trace its ownership through the Sleeth family of Belleville, New Jersey and Tucson, Arizona, before it passed by bequest to Robert G. Nelson and then to Martha Campbell Nelson, whose estate sold it. The auction house describes it as one of Heade’s extraordinary floral still lifes, painted around 1890 after the artist moved to St. Augustine, Florida.The estate went to courtThe estate’s representatives learned of the sale in February 1997. They first sued McKenzie-Larson, believing she was responsible for the loss, but settled that case after discovering she had no assets with which to pay damages. In late January 1998, the estate sued the Rices, seeking to rescind or reform the sale on the grounds of mutual mistake and unconscionability.The estate argued that neither party knew the transaction involved fine art. It claimed both sides believed they were dealing with relatively valueless wall decorations rather than valuable paintings. The Rices responded that the estate bore the risk of any mistake, that the doctrine of laches prevented reformation of the contract, and that unconscionability was not a proper basis for rescinding the sale.The trial court found that although both parties had been mistaken about the paintings’ value, the estate bore the risk of that mistake. It also found that the contract was not unconscionable because the parties had not negotiated the price. The estate had set the price, and Rice had simply paid it. The court denied the estate’s motion for summary judgment, granted the Rices’ cross motion, and later denied the estate’s request for a new trial.Why the Rices kept the windfallOn appeal, the estate argued that the mutual mistake should allow the sale to be rescinded. The Arizona Court of Appeals explained that a party seeking rescission must prove the claim by clear and convincing evidence. More importantly, the party asking for relief cannot bear the risk of the mistake. The court found that the estate did bear that risk.The personal representatives had hired two appraisers for the estate’s collection of Indian art and artifacts, but McKenzie-Larson had specifically said she did not appraise fine art. Newman testified that he was not concerned about her lack of expertise because he believed the estate contained nothing of significant value besides the house and the Indian art collection. Despite knowing that framed art existed beyond the Indian pieces, the representatives relied on someone admittedly unqualified to determine whether fine art was present.The appellate court characterized this as conscious ignorance. By choosing not to hire a qualified fine art appraiser, the estate knowingly proceeded despite its limited knowledge. The court also noted that the estate had ample opportunity to discover what it was selling and failed to do so, acting only after learning the paintings’ worth through the Rices’ own efforts. In the court’s view, the estate was a victim of its own folly, making it reasonable to allocate the burden of the mistake to the estate.A lesson in estate sale fortunesThe court also rejected the estate’s unconscionability argument. While the outcome may have seemed unfair in hindsight, the judges found that the terms of the contract were not. There had been no negotiation, the estate dictated the price for each painting, and Rice paid exactly what was asked. The court said it would be overly paternalistic to relieve a party from the consequences of what was, at worst, a bad bargain.The decision was affirmed in 2000, closing the legal chapter on one of the most remarkable estate sale discoveries in Arizona history. For collectors and casual shoppers alike, the case is a reminder that value is not always visible at first glance. A painting bought for $60 can turn out to be a museum quality work by Martin Johnson Heade, and a seller’s failure to investigate what it owns can carry a very expensive consequence.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1999, an Indiana woman bought a home with a $10,000 loan from her grandparents; 22 years later, her former partner's brother acquired half the property and tried to force a sale, but an appeals court let her keep it
articles.summary: A home bought with help from grandparents and maintained through decades of mortgage payments, repairs and household expenses became the centre of an
articles.body: A home bought with help from grandparents and maintained through decades of mortgage payments, repairs and household expenses became the centre of an unusual family property dispute in Indiana. More than two decades after purchasing the house, a woman found herself facing a demand to sell it from her former partner's brother, who had acquired a half-interest in the property. Despite having little financial involvement in the home, he sought to have it partitioned and sold. However, an appeals court has now upheld a decision allowing the woman to retain the entire property.In an October 29, 2026, opinion, available on Justia, the Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's ruling in Terry W Curella v. Gina A Behny. The court found no clear error in the decision to award the house to Gina Behny after considering her financial contributions over more than 25 years and the limited payments made by Terry Curella. The ruling also upheld a $4,307.95 monetary judgment against him, bringing the dispute over ownership and financial responsibility closer to resolution.A house bought with help from grandparentsThe dispute dates back to 1999, when Behny purchased a house in Kokomo, Indiana. To arrange the down payment, she borrowed $10,000 from her grandparents and financed the remaining $42,000 through a mortgage. Her boyfriend at the time, Gregg Curella, moved into the property with her. Around 2001, Behny needed additional money to pay an attorney in a child custody matter and carry out repairs to the house. Gregg agreed to co-sign a refinancing arrangement, increasing the mortgage from approximately $42,000 to $57,580.As part of the transaction, Behny signed a quitclaim deed transferring the property into joint ownership between herself and Gregg as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. Although Gregg eventually moved out in the autumn of 2004, his name remained on the property title. Behny, meanwhile, continued living in the house and taking responsibility for its expenses. She later lived there with her husband, Peter, and his disabled adult son.Former boyfriend's brother acquires a half-interestThe ownership dispute took a new turn in January 2021, when Gregg transferred his interest in the property to his brother, Terry Curella, through a quitclaim deed. The transfer was recorded on January 29, 2021, giving Terry an undivided half-interest in the house. Terry had never lived in the property. According to the court record, Gregg had lived there between 2001 and 2004 but had not made mortgage payments. Terry's financial involvement was also limited. He made one mortgage payment of $657.19 and one property tax payment of $456.64, which duplicated a payment already made through Behny's mortgage escrow.The ownership transfer also affected Behny's finances. After Terry's name was recorded on the title, she lost her homestead deduction, causing her monthly mortgage payment to increase by approximately $100 for two years. In April 2022, around 15 months after acquiring his interest, Terry petitioned the court to partition the property by sale. He submitted an appraisal valuing the house at $98,000 and sought to exercise his rights as a co-owner.Woman's $275,462 contribution becomes centralBehny opposed the proposed sale, arguing that she had carried the financial responsibility for the property over the years. Her contributions included mortgage payments, property taxes, homeowners' insurance, utilities, repairs and maintenance. She also paid for major improvements, including a new roof, furnace and water heater, bathroom repairs and a $1,000 insurance deductible following water damage.The trial court calculated her total contributions towards the property at $275,462.25. By comparison, Terry had made only two payments, both of which largely duplicated expenses already covered by Behny. Following a bench trial on August 28, 2024, the trial court concluded that requiring a sale would be grossly unfair. Although it granted Terry's petition for partition, the court awarded the entire property to Behny and directed him to transfer his interest to her through a quitclaim deed.Appeals court upholds the decisionTerry challenged the ruling before the Indiana Court of Appeals, questioning how the trial court had calculated the parties' respective contributions and why Behny was awarded the entire property. The appeals court acknowledged a procedural error involving the trial court's failure to include the parties' proposed findings and conclusions in the official record. However, it found that the error had not prejudiced Terry because the documents were available through the appeal record.On the ownership issue, the judges found that Terry had not demonstrated clear error in the trial court's decision. Even if Behny received only partial credit for several categories of her claimed expenses, her contributions would still substantially exceed the estimated value of Terry's half-interest, which was approximately $46,400 based on his appraisal.The court also upheld the monetary judgment, which included compensation for Behny's lost homestead deduction and addressed the treatment of a judgment lien against Terry. Although the lien had reached the end of its ten-year period before the final trial court judgment, the appeals court noted that the record did not establish whether any statutory exceptions applied. It found no error in the trial court's decision to place the associated financial risk on Terry.The Indiana Court of Appeals ultimately affirmed the lower court's judgment on October 29, 2026, allowing Behny to retain the house and requiring Terry to pay the $4,307.95 judgment. The decision brings attention to an important distinction in shared property ownership: holding a legal interest in a home does not necessarily settle how its value and financial contributions should be divided when a dispute reaches court. In this case, decades of payments, upkeep and investment proved central to determining who would keep the property.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Uttarakhand chopper crash: All six people on board chopper that crashed in Joshimath have died - what we know so far
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The six people on board a helicopter operated by Trans Bharat Aviation died after it crashed near Joshimath in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The six people on board a helicopter operated by Trans Bharat Aviation died after it crashed near Joshimath in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district on Friday afternoon. The helicopter was travelling from Badrinath to Dehradun when it crashed into a hillside near Chai village."All six people on board chopper that crashed in Joshimath have died, their bodies found," Chamoli Superintendent of Police Surjit Singh Panwar told PTI.The helicopter took off from Badrinath for Sahastradhara Heliport at 1.14 pm. Authorities lost track of it while it was crossing the Joshimath Valley and it was subsequently reported missing near Hathi Parvat.Search and rescue teams, including personnel from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), the Army, police and the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), were deployed to the area following reports of the crash.Flyers from Bengaluru; names of those on boardAccording to the available details, six people were on board the helicopter, including the pilot and five passengers, all reportedly from Bengaluru. Their identities are as follows:Pilot: Captain HimanshuPassengers:Prathapa (Male)Arun (Male)Shankar Gowda (Male)Sudheer K (Male)H S Natraja (Male)Helicopter lost contact while crossing Joshimath Speaking to PTI in Dehradun, Prateek Jain, CEO of the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA), said "the helicopter took off from Badrinath for Sahastradhara Heliport at 1.14 pm today. As it was crossing the Joshimath Valley, we suddenly lost track of it on our tracking system, which we use to monitor its movements. We have also received some local information regarding the incident.""So far, nothing has been confirmed. However, according to the information available in the passenger manifest, a total of six people were on board the helicopter, the pilot and five passengers. The helicopter's location has not yet been traced. However, search and rescue teams have been mobilised in coordination with the Chamoli district administration," he said."The SDRF has also been deployed, along with a unit of the Army. As soon as the weather clears, we will send another rescue helicopter from here to locate the missing helicopter," Jain added.Local inputs about the incident also prompted authorities to initiate a search operation.Chopper showing near Army Camp above Chai villageSub-Inspector Manohar Kanyal of Joshimath police post said information about the incident was received from the Joshimath sub-divisional magistrate (SDM) at 2.21 pm."At 14:21 hrs, information was received from the SDM Joshimath regarding the crash landing of a helicopter above Chai village in the Joshimath area," Kanyal told ANI."In this regard, UCADA officials stated that the location of a Trans Bharat helicopter, which was flying from Badrinath to Sahastradhara, is showing near the Army Camp above Chai village. Complete details regarding the crash or crash landing are not yet available," he added.Entire Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter fleet groundedSpeaking to ANI, Jain said the helicopter belonged to Trans Bharat Aviation and confirmed that the company’s entire fleet had been grounded as a precautionary measure."A helicopter belonging to Trans Bharat Aviation departed from Badrinath for the Sahastradhara heliport at 1:14 PM. We have been unable to trace the helicopter's location since it was passing through the vicinity of the Joshimath valley. Upon receiving this information, we mobilised the Chamoli district administration, the SDRF (State Disaster Response Force), and an Army unit to the area near the incident site to prepare for a proper rescue operation," he said."As a precautionary measure, the entire fleet of helicopters belonging to Trans Bharat Aviation has been grounded...According to initial information, there were 6 people on board—the pilot plus 5 others. We will share further details once we have confirmation..." he added.The grounding is a precautionary step as authorities work to establish the circumstances surrounding the crash.Rescue teams deployed near Chai villageUttarakhand disaster management officials in Chamoli district said teams had rushed to the area to conduct search and rescue operations. Police, SDRF, Army and ITBP personnel were dispatched to the reported crash site.The location of the helicopter and the condition of the people on board remained unclear in the initial hours after the incident. Authorities were coordinating with the district administration and other agencies to locate the aircraft and assess the situation.It was also not immediately confirmed whether the helicopter was returning after ferrying pilgrims from the Badrinath shrine.CM Pushkar Singh Dhami monitors situationUttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said he was closely monitoring the situation and that a joint rescue operation was under way.In a post on X, Dhami said, "Reports have been received regarding an unfortunate helicopter crash near Chai village, close to Joshimath. A joint rescue operation is being conducted by the district administration, the Disaster Management Department, and the SDRF.""I am personally monitoring the situation closely. I have issued instructions to ensure that those who are critically injured are immediately airlifted to a higher-level medical facility for better treatment. I pray to God for the safety of the passengers," Dhami added.The state government said the rescue operation was being coordinated by the district administration and disaster management authorities.Uttarakhand sees heavy rain, snowfallThe crash took place amid adverse weather conditions in Uttarakhand, with rainfall and snowfall reported in several parts of the state.Television channels reported that fire and smoke were visible at the crash site and that rescue teams had reached the area. Bad weather was suspected to have contributed to the incident, though the cause had not been officially established.Kedarnath Dham witnessed the season's first heavy snowfall following continuous snowfall since Thursday, October 29. The surrounding hills were covered in snow, while temperatures in the region dropped significantly.The India Meteorological Department's Dehradun centre also forecast continued rainfall over the next few days, particularly in the hill districts.Rain forecast over the next few daysDr CS Tomar, director of the Meteorological Centre in Dehradun, said heavy rainfall had been recorded at eight to nine places across Uttarakhand on October 29, particularly in Uttarkashi, Tehri and Haridwar districts.Tomar said similar weather conditions were expected on Friday, with a higher likelihood of rainfall in the Kumaon region."Tomorrow, on the 31st, chances of light to very light rain will persist, especially in the hilly districts. Similarly, on the 1st and 2nd (of November), light to very light rain may be witnessed at isolated places, particularly in our northern hilly districts," he said.In view of the forecast, district administrations have been placed on alert to ensure the safety of pilgrims, residents and commuters.Earlier on Thursday, District Magistrate Prashant Arya directed officials to activate the District Emergency Operations Centre (DEOC) in alert mode to monitor weather conditions and oversee precautionary measures.Authorities are also monitoring road conditions and the Gangotri and Yamunotri shrines through live CCTV cameras.The administration has appealed to devotees and pilgrims to take precautions against the cold and follow advisories issued by the administration and police.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'They plotted': Ex-Manipur CM Biren Singh blames BJP leaders for ouster, questions continued violence
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Manipur chief minister N Biren Singh has accused sections of the state BJP leadership of conspiring with the Congress to remove him from
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Manipur chief minister N Biren Singh has accused sections of the state BJP leadership of conspiring with the Congress to remove him from office. Singh also questioned the continued violence in the state since his resignation in February 2025.In an exclusive interview with PTI, Singh said the BJP government must urgently work to "regain the lost confidence and trust of the people" ahead of assembly elections due early next year. He also claimed there was strong public demand for his return as chief minister."I had not been treated well since 2017. I am not accusing the Delhi leadership but sections of the state leaders who conspired against me with the Congress,” Singh told PTI. He alleged that some party colleagues resented his elevation despite having switched from the Congress to the BJP.“There are MLAs who could never accept how I became CM twice after having crossed over from the Congress. They consider BJP as their property. So they plotted, planned and made me resign," he added.Singh also challenged the argument that his removal would help restore peace in the state, pointing to continuing clashes involving Meitei, Kuki and Naga communities. The present government, led by Y Khemchand Singh, took office in February this year."Now Biren is out. So, what happened now? How many Naga brothers have died? They were blaming me. They were saying I favour the majority. Now it is Christians versus Christians. Where has the European Union gone?" he asked.His remarks come amid renewed violence in the state. Three Meitei villagers were shot dead and three others injured in an ambush by suspected militants inside a forest along the Imphal East-Kangpokpi border on Monday. The victims were part of a group collecting firewood near Nongshum and Khongbal Tangkhul villages when the attack took place.The killings triggered protests in Imphal, with demonstrators carrying the bodies of two victims to a sit-in outside the chief minister's official residence. Security personnel later used tear gas to disperse the crowd. The latest killings come amid escalating clashes between Kuki-Zo and Naga groups in the hill districts, with more than 50 people reportedly killed on either side over the past eight months.Expressing concern over the BJP's declining public confidence, Singh also questioned the government's commitment to issues that had featured prominently during his tenure, including the anti-drug campaign and action against illegal immigration."That is my main worry," he told PTI when asked whether public anxiety could hurt the BJP in the elections."Anti-drug campaign, anti-poppy plantation, that campaign we are not seeing. The government should also continue biometric identification of suspected illegal immigrants. At least identify them. And even if you can't deport the illegal immigrants at least you can keep them in camps. What we have started, continue it. And save the future. We have to save the future," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2005, two art dealers bought a damaged painting with a Leonardo da Vinci connection for just $1,175; 12 years later, it sold for a world record $450 million
articles.summary: In 2005, two art dealers bought an old painting of Jesus Christ at an auction in New Orleans for $1,175.
articles.body: In 2005, two art dealers bought an old painting of Jesus Christ at an auction in New Orleans for $1,175. The work was in poor condition and had been attributed to a follower of Leonardo da Vinci, rather than the Renaissance master himself. Twelve years later, the same painting sold for $450.3 million at Christie's in New York, setting a record for the most expensive painting ever sold at auction.The painting, known as ‘Salvator Mundi,’ meaning ‘Saviour of the World,’ became one of the art market's biggest stories. Its dramatic rise in value followed years of restoration, historical research and expert examination. But its attribution to Leonardo has remained contested, and the painting has not been publicly displayed since its planned unveiling at the Louvre Abu Dhabi was postponed in 2018.Its journey raises two questions: how did a painting once dismissed as a copy become a record-breaking work, and who actually painted it?A painting that disappeared from history‘Salvator Mundi’ depicts Christ facing forward, raising his right hand in blessing while holding a transparent crystal orb in his left. The composition is associated with the Christian image of Christ as the saviour of the world. The painting is generally dated to around 1500, although its precise date and authorship remain debated.According to the official website of British auction house Christie's, the painting belonged to King Charles I of England and was recorded in an inventory of the royal collection drawn up in 1650, a year after his execution. Its whereabouts between 1763 and 1900 are not fully documented.In 1900, the painting entered the Cook Collection in England after being acquired from Sir Charles Robinson, who had purchased it as a work by Bernardino Luini, an artist associated with Leonardo's circle. In 1958, the painting was sold at Sotheby's in London for just £45. The auction catalogue attributed it to Giovanni Boltraffio, another painter associated with Leonardo's circle. After the sale, the work again remained out of public view for decades.Next major turning point came in April 2005The next major turning point came in April 2005. According to research by art historian Frank Zöllner, the work appeared at an auction at the St Charles Gallery in New Orleans. It was catalogued as a work after Leonardo da Vinci. Art dealers Robert Simon and Alexander Parish acquired it for a total of $1,175, including the buyer's premium, after a hammer price of $1,000.At that point, it was not being sold as an undiscovered Leonardo masterpiece. It was a damaged old painting whose true artistic significance had yet to be established.Restoration changed the painting's storyAfter the 2005 purchase, the painting underwent extensive conservation under Dianne Dwyer Modestini. The restoration, carried out from 2007, helped reveal details that had been obscured by layers of old paint, dirt and previous interventions. The process also exposed the difficulties of assessing a work that had suffered significant damage. Parts of the panel and painted surface were in poor condition, and some areas required careful reconstruction.The restoration was followed by years of research. Experts examined the composition, drawing beneath the paint, materials and relationship between the work and other versions of Salvator Mundi. In 2011, London's National Gallery included it in an exhibition devoted to Leonardo da Vinci, presenting it as a work by the artist. That exhibition was a decisive moment.From $1,175 to $127.5 millionThe painting's value rose sharply after its attribution gained recognition. In May 2013, Swiss art dealer Yves Bouvier acquired it through a private sale for $83 million. He subsequently sold it to Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev for $127.5 million. The difference between the two prices later became part of a legal dispute between Rybolovlev and Bouvier. Rybolovlev accused the dealer of misleading him about transactions involving artworks, including the prices at which they had been acquired. Bouvier denied wrongdoing. Their dispute became one of the art market's most prominent legal battles and was settled in 2023.Rybolovlev eventually decided to sell Salvator Mundi. Christie's placed it in its Post-War and Contemporary Art evening sale in New York on November 15, 2017, rather than in a traditional Old Masters auction.The decision helped bring the painting before a global audience of major collectors. Christie's reported that nearly 30,000 people visited exhibitions of the work in Hong Kong, London, San Francisco and New York before the sale. The auction lasted around 19 minutes. The hammer fell at $400 million, and the final price, including the buyer's premium, reached $450,312,500.According to Christie's, the sale broke the previous auction record for a work of art by a wide margin. Guinness World Records also lists ‘Salvator Mundi’ as the most expensive painting sold at auction.Why experts still disagreeThe record price did not end the debate over the painting's authorship. Some specialists believe Leonardo painted the work himself, while others argue that it was produced largely by an assistant or in his workshop, perhaps using a design by the master. Bernardino Luini and Giovanni Boltraffio, both associated with Leonardo's circle, have been mentioned in discussions of the painting.The disagreement is partly rooted in the painting's condition. Extensive restoration makes it difficult to determine how much of the visible surface belongs to the original artist and how much reflects later work. The debate is not simply about whether the painting is a Leonardo or a copy. Some specialists believe that Leonardo may have contributed to parts of the work while assistants from his workshop executed other sections.Where is the $450 million painting now?After the 2017 sale, the identity of the buyer remained uncertain for a time. Prince Badr bin Abdullah al-Saud was identified as the successful bidder. Christie's subsequently confirmed that Abu Dhabi's Department of Culture and Tourism was acquiring the painting. However, later reports linked the purchase to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, with Prince Badr reportedly acting on his behalf.The painting was expected to be displayed at the Louvre Abu Dhabi in September 2018, but the planned unveiling was postponed without a public explanation. It was also absent from the Louvre in Paris's major 2019 Leonardo exhibition.An August 2024 report by The Guardian said Princeton academic Bernard Haykel had been told by Saudi culture minister Prince Badr that the painting was being kept in a secure vault in Geneva until a museum in Riyadh was completed. The report also examined suggestions that it could eventually become a centrepiece of a future Saudi museum. However, its present location has not been independently confirmed.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, Indiana University opened a free AI course to its alumni network of 805,000 people; more than 114,000 learners had already enrolled
articles.summary: Indiana University has expanded access to its free generative artificial intelligence course after seeing strong interest from its students, employees and
articles.body: Indiana University has expanded access to its free generative artificial intelligence course after seeing strong interest from its students, employees and alumni. Initially developed to help members of the university community understand and use AI, the online programme has since attracted more than 114,000 enrolments. The university first extended the opportunity to its large alumni network before opening the course to people worldwide in April 2026, making university-level AI training available to a much wider audience without charging a course fee.Indiana University’s free AI course reached more than 114,000 learnersIndiana University introduced GenAI 101 as part of its efforts to build practical AI skills across its community. The course was designed to help participants understand generative AI and use it more confidently in everyday tasks, academic work and professional settings.According to a report published by Indiana Public Media in April 2026, the course had recorded more than 114,000 enrolments since its launch in August. These included students, faculty members and university staff. The university subsequently expanded access to more than 800,000 alumni worldwide in October, bringing the learning opportunity to people who had already graduated but wanted to develop their knowledge of emerging technology.The expansion reflected growing interest in AI education beyond university classrooms. People from outside Indiana University had also contacted Brian Williams, a professor at the Kelley School of Business who helped develop the programme, expressing interest in taking the course.What makes the GenAI 101 programme differentThe course was developed by faculty and staff at the Kelley School of Business, Indiana University’s business school. Its aim was to make AI knowledge accessible to people from different academic and professional backgrounds rather than limiting it to technology specialists.GenAI 101 consists of 8 self-paced modules containing 16 lessons. Each module focuses on practical applications, allowing learners to build their understanding gradually and apply what they learn to real situations.The programme covers several important areas of AI use, including prompt engineering, data storytelling, fact-checking AI-generated information and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. Prompt engineering involves giving AI tools clear instructions so that they can produce more relevant and useful responses.The course also addresses the importance of checking information produced by AI systems. Although these tools can generate answers quickly, their responses are not always accurate. Learning to assess the information before relying on it is therefore an important part of developing AI skills.Indiana University also highlights three main learning areas: foundational prompt engineering, using AI as a thought partner and treating AI as a productivity tool. Together, these areas are intended to help participants use the technology for problem-solving, developing ideas and completing tasks more efficiently.How does the course help learners use AI in everyday workOne of the programme's notable features is its conversational AI learning assistant, named Crimson. It provides real-time support to participants as they work through the lessons, giving them an opportunity to interact with an AI system while learning about the technology itself.The Kelley School explains that Crimson is designed as an animated AI co-teacher. It demonstrates how learners can question, challenge and engage with generative AI rather than simply accepting everything it produces.This practical approach is also reflected in the tools used throughout the programme. According to the Kelley School, the course includes examples based on publicly accessible generative AI platforms, including Google Gemini and ChatGPT. This allows participants to connect the lessons with tools they may already encounter in their personal or professional lives.The course was also designed to be approachable. Brian Williams, the Sam Frumer Professor of Accounting and chair of the Kelley School's Virtual Advanced Business Technologies Department, said the team used short instructional videos with some humour to make a complicated and rapidly developing subject easier to understand.Williams told Indiana Public Media that feedback from learners had been positive. Participants ranged from first-year university students to executives working at major companies. Their responses suggested that the course helped make AI concepts more understandable and useful in practical situations.Why did Indiana University decide to make the course free worldwideThe decision to open GenAI 101 to the public followed growing interest from people and organisations outside the university. Williams told Indiana Public Media that he had received emails from people in Indiana and other parts of the United States asking whether they could take the course.The Kelley School of Business also reported that businesses, state governments and universities across the country had approached Indiana University about obtaining or developing similar AI training programmes. This interest encouraged the university and the business school to make their existing course available to everyone without a fee.The public launch took place on April 16, 2026. According to Indiana Public Media's report published the following day, around 500 people enrolled during the first 5 hours after public registration opened.Cost was another important consideration behind the decision. Williams pointed out that some AI certification programmes can cost between $1,500 and $5,000. Making GenAI 101 free offered people an opportunity to develop relevant skills without having to pay substantial fees for training.The move also reflects changes taking place in the employment market. In its announcement, the Kelley School cited an expectation that 90% of employers would implement AI solutions by 2028. Its dean, Pat Hopkins, stressed that understanding artificial intelligence was becoming an increasingly important professional skill.The university explains that the programme is available through IU Expand, with the university's students, faculty and staff having access through their institutional accounts.You use AI every day. articles.title: Melinda French Gates has a 2-day rule for employees, she says that if they pass this, they can be confident that the job they did was good
articles.summary: Melinda French Gates has said she follows a 2-day rule for her employees.
articles.body: Melinda French Gates has said she follows a 2-day rule for her employees. She explained that if their work passes the 48-hour test, they can be confident that they have done a good job. Speaking with Bloomberg’s Leaders With Francine Lacqua podcast in March earlier this year, Melinda French Gates shared her secret formula for handling conflict at work. “If I’m unhappy with work you have done, you will hear from me within 48 hours,” she said during the interview adding “I’m not going to tell you right away, because I need time to think it through.” Gates said that she does to ‘calm down’.“If they pass the 48-hour mark, they can be confident that the job they did was a good job,” she said. “You’re not going to get to your performance review and have a surprise.”Melinda French Gates on the logic behind 48-hour feedback ruleMelinda French Gates has been practicing the 48-hour feedback philosophy for decades. Gates cochaired the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation from 2000 until she stepped down in 2024. She explained that the practice is not about avoiding criticism, but about giving it with honesty, integrity and grace.“Being clear is kind,” French Gates said, “because I’m giving them feedback so they can actually grow and become better.”Gates described her 48-hour feedback mantra as maintaining integrity while keeping the other person’s dignity intact: “gracious, thoughtful, before you go into it.” “I don’t mind conflict,” she told Bloomberg then. “I learned to do it in a way for me that maintained my integrity.”Melinda French Gates pledges $215 million for women’s healthEarlier this month, Melinda Gates pledged $215 million in new funding for women’s health and called for greater accountability in addressing long-standing gaps in healthcare for women, saying progress should be measured over the next four to five years to determine whether access to treatment is improving. Speaking in a Bloomberg Television interview in London, French Gates said the world remains significantly behind in addressing women's health needs and argued that governments must invest more in research, prevention and data collection."We are way behind on women's health across the world," French Gates said, adding that better evidence is needed to persuade policymakers to prioritise the issue and direct resources where they can have the greatest impact. "Measuring matters," she said. "Let's come back and measure this in four or five years" to assess whether women are better able to access treatments and healthcare support.You use AI every day. articles.title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into  Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell Balmoral visits
articles.summary: The force said it had received information and stressed its inquiries were at "an early stage".
articles.body:
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.

The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.

Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking , are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.

Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.

The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.

Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.

"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.

"We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.

At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.

Prince Andrew hosted Epstein, Maxwell and Weinstein at Royal Lodge

Email by 'A' from 'Balmoral' asked Ghislaine Maxwell for 'inappropriate friends', Epstein files show

According to the Express, flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.

An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.

It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.

Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.

Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".

The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."

Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".

Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.

Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.

Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.

In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office , in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.

Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.

Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

articles.title: A Tennessee husband claimed the marital home was worth up to $300,000 during the divorce, but the court valued it at $160,400 and awarded 75% of its equity to his wife; an October 27 appeal upheld the division
articles.summary: A Tennessee appeals court has upheld a trial court’s decision to value the marital home at $160,400 and award the wife 75% of its equity.
articles.body: A Tennessee appeals court has upheld a trial court’s decision to value the marital home at $160,400 and award the wife 75% of its equity. In a ruling filed on October 27, 2026, the court rejected the husband’s challenge to the valuation and the division. The court found that the record supported the lower figure, even though the husband had offered comparable sales ranging from $310,000 to $350,000. The ruling did not settle everything, however. The court vacated the values assigned to his artwork and tools and sent the parenting plan back for new findings.Two price tags for one homeThe couple married in Texas in 2015 and moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, about a year later. The wife was the primary provider throughout their marriage. The couple welcomed their first child, a son, in July 2017. The child had autism and developmental delays. Five years later, they separated, and the husband filed for divorce in 2024. At trial, he valued the house at “slightly north of $300,000”. To support that figure, he pointed to three nearby homes that had sold for $310,000, $320,000 and $350,000.The real value of the marital home The couple bought the house, which was built in 1945, in 2018. They paid $109,000. The wife testified that it could be worth about $200,000, but only after major repairs to the heating system and roof. She also submitted photographs showing the condition of the home and other defects. The county property assessor had valued the house at $160,400.Following the separation, the husband insisted that the property was worth more. The trial court described his estimate as “greatly inflated” and noted that the comparable homes he cited were not truly comparable in size, condition or lot. The appeals court agreed that the record supported the lower figure. It also said that a judge does not err simply by believing one side over the other, as long as the final value falls within the evidence presented.Based on these findings, the wife was awarded 75% of the equity. The total equity in the marital home came to $62,852.84, meaning the wife would receive $47,139.21. The husband’s 25% share was approximately $15,713.21.The state’s law requires courts to weigh each spouse’s contributions, including work as a homemaker, wage earner or parent. The statute says those roles count equally, but only if both spouses actually fulfilled their responsibilities. The trial court found that the wife worked throughout the marriage and was the main caregiver for their son, who has significant developmental needs. It also found that the husband handled homemaking duties for only about four years. The court heard testimony about occasions when his drinking left the child unsupervised. The appeals court said the record did not contradict those findings.The husband also owed about $20,000 in back child support, and a magistrate had set a repayment plan of $55 a month, which would have taken more than 30 years to complete. The trial court ordered the debt to be paid in full from his share of the marital estate. The husband argued that the court could not change the payment plan because neither side had appealed it. However, the appeals court rejected that argument. It explained that the judgment fixed the total amount owed, while the payment schedule only governed how quickly he had to pay it. It is not unusual for courts to change the schedule, especially when it becomes unreasonable.The ruling should not be considered a clean win for either side. The appeals court vacated the trial court’s $2,000 valuations for the husband’s original artwork and tools because neither party had offered evidence of their value. The trial court must now exclude those values from the property division and recalculate each spouse’s share. The court also vacated the permanent parenting plan. Its order did not explain how it weighed the child’s best interests or why the restrictions on the husband’s visits were necessary. The appeals court said it could only guess at the reasoning and declined to simply adopt the husband’s proposed plan. The current arrangement stays in place until a new one is entered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Boston Celtics owners donate over $200 million to children's hospital after one billionaire couple's $100 million pledge inspired others to match their gift; the money will fund mental health care, medical research and nursing training
articles.summary: The ownership group of the Boston Celtics has joined forces to donate more than $200 million to Boston Children's Hospital, marking the largest gift in
articles.body: The ownership group of the Boston Celtics has joined forces to donate more than $200 million to Boston Children's Hospital, marking the largest gift in the institution's history. The record-breaking contribution follows an earlier $100 million pledge by billionaire philanthropists Rob and Karen Hale, which reportedly inspired fellow owners to match their commitment. Announced on October 29, 2026, the donation will support several healthcare priorities, including the expansion of paediatric mental health services, research into childhood diseases, advanced training for paediatric nurses and programmes supporting children and families. The gift brings together professional basketball, private philanthropy and children's healthcare, with the funding intended to strengthen medical care and research while helping the hospital respond to the complex needs of young patients.How one couple's $100 million pledge inspired a bigger giftRob Hale, a telecommunications entrepreneur and member of the Celtics' ownership group, and his wife, Karen, announced their $100 million commitment to Boston Children's Hospital in December 2025. The money was intended to help establish a major paediatric behavioural health campus in Brighton, Boston, addressing the need for expanded mental health services for children and adolescents.Their contribution became the starting point for a larger collective commitment. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, the Hales' pledge inspired other members of the Celtics' ownership group to match their contribution, taking the overall gift to more than $200 million.The announcement did not disclose how much each owner contributed individually. The combined donation represents a major expansion of philanthropic support for the hospital and builds on the Hales' earlier commitment to improving children's mental healthcare.Mental health care at the centre of the donationA major priority is the development of a paediatric behavioural health campus in Brighton, Boston, intended to improve access to specialised mental health services for children and adolescents. The project, being developed on the grounds of Franciscan Children's, is designed to bring different levels of care together, including inpatient treatment and intensive outpatient programmes.The planned campus is part of a wider effort to address the demand for children's psychiatric care and encourage earlier intervention for young patients experiencing mental health crises. The project is valued at approximately $640 million, according to The Boston Globe. The new facility is expected to expand the hospital's capacity to care for children with complex behavioural health needs.Research into childhood diseases and future treatmentsAnother priority is funding research into emerging therapies for childhood diseases and investigating the origins of diseases that affect adults. Boston Children's Hospital has a major research operation, with scientists working on conditions ranging from common illnesses to rare and complex disorders.The new funding is intended to help researchers explore potential treatments and develop approaches that could improve patient outcomes. It will also support an innovation fund designed to encourage new ideas capable of transforming children's healthcare. The hospital has not publicly detailed the specific research projects that will receive support.Advanced training for paediatric nursesThe donation will also support advanced training for paediatric nurses, strengthening the skills of professionals who provide specialised care to children. Nurses play an important role in treating young patients, monitoring their recovery and supporting families through difficult medical circumstances.By investing in professional development alongside research and facilities, the gift aims to strengthen several parts of the healthcare system. The hospital has not announced how many nurses will benefit from the training or how much of the donation will be allocated to this initiative.Family programmes and community healthThe remaining priorities include expanding family-centred programmes that encourage healthy lifestyles in local communities. These initiatives are intended to extend the impact of the hospital's work beyond clinical treatment, helping children and families access programmes that support their health and wellbeing.The donation will also give the hospital greater scope to explore new approaches to paediatric care through its innovation fund. Together, these initiatives reflect a broader focus on prevention, research and treatment, rather than concentrating exclusively on hospital facilities.Celtics ownership says the legacy goes beyond basketballBoston Celtics chairman and governor Bill Chisholm said the contribution reflected the belief that a team's legacy should extend beyond its achievements on the court. He described the donation as a commitment to the next generation in Boston and beyond.Boston Children's Hospital chief executive Dr Kevin Churchwell said the gift's significance would ultimately be measured by the lives it saves rather than the record it sets. He said the contribution would help the institution expand its work with children and families and accelerate efforts to improve care.The Celtics have also maintained a wider community-giving programme through the Boston Celtics Shamrock Foundation, established in 2004. The hospital donation represents a major additional commitment to healthcare and research, bringing together the team's ownership group, the franchise and its philanthropic arm.About Boston Children's HospitalFounded in 1869, Boston Children's Hospital is a paediatric teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School. It provides specialised medical care for children and adolescents and conducts research into diseases affecting both young patients and adults.The hospital operates a broad network of clinical programmes and satellite locations, serving patients from across the US and other countries. Its research teams work on preventing, treating and potentially curing diseases, including rare and complex conditions.The record donation is expected to support this work across several areas, from mental health services and nursing education to research and family programmes, giving the hospital additional resources to pursue improvements in children's healthcare.You use AI every day.
